chapter: Woody Herman, Condon's and Buddy Rich
title: Glenn Miller band, public-domain hits and royalties
summary: Why the Glenn Miller band continues, what he learned from DeFranco, and the film royalties he receives.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Isn’t that something? Yeah, he had a less personalized sound.
Who is that Glenn Miller? © Fillius Jazz Archive -26-

Well I wouldn’t say that because he had that clarinet lead. But the thing is that he was smart and half of the tunes that he made popular were public domain. “Little Brown Jug,” “American Patrol,” I can’t remember all of them but he didn’t have to pay any royalties on those tunes you know, so I mean he made a fortune. I mean well of course there’s some different opinions on that. Some people say that Glenn Miller should have lived and his music should have died. Other people say that he should have — the plane should have gone down with him and the music in it — you know, certain guys. But I mean I enjoyed playing with the band. I learned a lot, because Buddy DeFranco was so strict you know, like with the thing. So I did learn a lot from playing with that band. And that thing right there, that’s a plaque of a platitude — we did a Glenn Miller “In the Mood” — that’s a million is it? Seller. And we did three of them and it’s gone triple platinum of the three of them. So that’s what that — “In the Christmas Mood.”
Do you get payments, royalties, for any of the stuff you’ve done?

Not for that. That thing I get royalties because they used some of that the music in, well Sandra Bullock’s “While You Were Sleeping” and there was another one I think called “The Little” — how do you say it, “Fockers?” Or the little something.
Oh yeah, “Meet the Fockers” or something, the second one.
They used some of that, music for that, and I get some minor royalties from that.
